query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Cocktail Effect–Driven Passivation Layer Formation Hypothesis
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, homogeneous lightweight HEA with a carefully selected elemental cocktail including traditional oxide-formers (e.g., Al, Cr) alongside low-density components.
generation.intervention: Optimize the alloy’s elemental composition to maximize the formation of continuous, self-healing passivating oxide layers during service, while preserving the low density.
generation.conditions: Expose samples to high-temperature oxidation environments (800–1400 °C) and corrosive media (e.g., 0.6 M or 3.5% NaCl solutions) while monitoring mechanical integrity under cyclical loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent and adherent multi-component passivation film (incorporating oxides such as Al2O3, Cr2O3, and possibly mixed oxides) on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The ‘cocktail effect’ in HEAs—whereby the synergistic combination of multiple elements—promotes the in situ formation of a dense, protective oxide scale. This passivation layer not only slows further oxidation and corrosion by limiting elemental diffusion but also reinforces the surface mechanically, contributing to overall high strength and durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline HEA lacking optimal oxide-forming elements, the optimized composition is predicted to exhibit lower corrosion current densities (e.g., reductions to the order of 10^(-8) A/cm²) and reduced high-temperature oxidation weight gains (e.g., an order of magnitude improvement) while maintaining or enhancing mechanical strength.
generation.baseline: HEA alloys with similar low density but without the optimized balance of oxide-forming elements.
generation.boundary: If the operating temperature exceeds the stability range of the passivation layers, or if cyclic thermal stresses disrupt film continuity, the protective mechanism may fail.
generation.uncertainty: Long-term durability of the complex passivation film under service conditions and thermal cycling remains to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two HEA compositions: one optimized for forming continuous oxide layers by enhancing the content of Al and Cr, and one with a conventional composition. Subject both to prolonged high-temperature oxidation tests and corrosion testing in NaCl solution while assessing the integrity of passivation films via surface analysis (e.g., XPS and SEM).
measurements: Surface oxide composition and continuity (XPS, SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized alloy does not show statistically significant enhanced passivation (i.e., no marked improvement in oxidation or corrosion resistance) relative to the baseline, or if the oxide film fails to remain coherent during testing, the hypothesis would be invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: In the present study, six types of NbTi-bearing RMEAs and RHEAs were fabricated. The relationship between element effects, oxidation and segregation was discussed among these alloys. A higher content of Cr was beneficial due to the formation of continuous CrNbO4 and Cr2O3. Due to the segregation of Ti, TiO2 was mainly present in the interdendritic region. Mo and Ta segregated to the dendritic region, and Ta exhibited a detrimental effect on oxidation resistance in most cases. The dilution of the protective elements and segregation made the formation of a protective oxide layer during oxidation difficult. The effect of Mo addition on oxidation varied depending on the type of oxide layer present. In the presence of a protective oxide layer, low oxygen solubility could enhance oxidation resistance. However, in the absence of a protective oxide layer, the segregation of Mo could result in the formation of voids due to Mo-oxide evaporation. In this work, NbTi + AlCrMo showed good oxidation at a high temperature and low density. It can be a candidate for next-generation materials for high-temperature applications, such as aerospace and gas turbines.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), a novel class of multi-principal element alloys, brought a new era in the study of alloy materials []. The presence of five or more elements in close proximity to the iso-atomic ratio endows alloys with high configurational entropy, which confers upon HEAs the capacity to form stable simple solid solution phases. This, in turn, endows HEAs with exceptional mechanical properties and commendable corrosion resistance []. This property gives high-entropy alloys excellent mechanical and physical properties, including high strength, high fracture toughness, and the ability to conduct electricity at very low temperatures []. In addition, they exhibit excellent resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Consequently, in the aerospace field [], where the temperature of service varies widely, in the field of ultra-high temperature structural materials [], in marine industrial equipment [], and in the nuclear industry [], where there are harsh working conditions, high-entropy alloys have a wider range of application prospects than traditional alloys due to their rich elemental composition and flexible selection of elemental content.
